Thunder shook the stonecutter so hard loose stones rattled in the wall, but everyone near me is still standing.
I checked walls, steps, and cracked blocks after the lightning, then counted heads. No one should be alone after a sky like that.
Near the stonecutter, the bell sounded small under that thunder. We stayed inside and kept the doors watched.
That thunder made everyone quiet. I checked the doorframes twice.
The sky can keep its lightning. I have doorframes to set right.
I checked wooden beams set into stone for sparks first, then checked faces for smoke and fear.
We passed water hand to hand and kept people away from the smoke. I checked the stonecutter after.
The stonecutter can wait. People come first.

During a raid, the stonecutter can sit silent; who makes it behind a door matters more.

We counted living neighbors before walls, steps, and cracked blocks. That is the only count worth starting with.
Raiders came looking for easy emeralds. They found barred doors near the stonecutter and a bell that would not stop ringing.
From the stonecutter, I saw fear cross the square; then I saw courage get there first.
Night trouble tests the loose latch by the stonecutter first. We are fixing those before sunset.
I stayed near the wall with the missing block and listened for anyone calling from the dark.

The dark tested everyone. Most of us passed by keeping a stack of spare stone between us and teeth.

The wind threw sand through every crack. I am still cleaning sand from the mortar lines.
I checked walls, steps, and cracked blocks, then checked who was coughing too hard to answer.
Sand reached the stonecutter, the hinges, and half our eyes, but no one has been reported missing.
